title: Linear Approximation
body:
Replace a curve near a point by its tangent line:

$$
f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) \qquad\text{for } x \text{ near } a
$$

This is the **whole content of the [[Derivative]]** stated as a formula: the derivative is the
slope of the best straight-line fit at a point, and this is that line being used for arithmetic.
$\sqrt{4.1} \approx 2 + \frac{1}{4}(0.1) = 2.025$, against a true value of $2.0248...$, using
nothing but the tangent at $x = 4$.

The **differential** notation is the same statement rearranged: $dy = f'(x)\,dx$, read as "a small
change in $x$ produces roughly $f'(x)$ times that change in $y$". It is where $\frac{dy}{dx}$ gets
away with looking like a fraction, and why the [[Chain Rule]] and [[U-Substitution]] can be
manipulated as if the $du$'s cancel.

The approximation is good near $a$ and degrades as you move away, at a rate governed by $f''$: a
nearly straight function stays accurate for a long way, a sharply curved one does not.
[[Taylor Series]] in [[CALCULUS 2]] is this idea kept going, adding $\frac{f''(a)}{2}(x-a)^2$ and
so on, with linear approximation as the degree-1 truncation.

## Why it is the organising idea of the course

Every application in Calc 1 is this approximation being read for information. [[Related Rates]]
propagates it forward in time, [[Curve Sketching]] reads its slope and its bend, [[Optimization]]
looks for where it goes flat, and [[Riemann Sum|integration]] approximates area by treating $f$ as
constant over each tiny interval, which is the degree-0 version of the same move. **Calculus is
local linear approximation**, and everything else is bookkeeping.

It is also why linear algebra and calculus meet in [[MACHINE LEARNING]]: a
[[Gradient|gradient step]] is a linear approximation to a loss surface, taken at a point, trusted
only for a short distance. The learning rate is exactly the "how far can I trust this before the
curvature bites" question.
